title: If you declare a local variable inside main() but do not initialize it and then try to print it, what happens and why?
shortTitle: What happens if you print an uninitialized local variable?
keyPoints: The code does not compile: you get "variable might not have been initialized"
Local variables receive no default value, unlike instance fields which default to 0/false/null
Java enforces definite assignment: the compiler proves every local is assigned on every path before it is read
Assigning on only one branch of an if still fails if the other branch does not assign
A branch that throws or returns is pruned from the analysis, so the surviving path is enough
This catches bugs at compile time rather than at runtime with a wrong value

s1_definition.oneliner: It does not compile. Local variables get no default value, and Java's definite-assignment rule rejects any read of a local that has not been assigned on every possible path.
s1_definition.profdef:
Three facts explain what happens:

- **No default.** Unlike instance variables (which default to 0, false, or null), local variables are never given a default value by the compiler.
- **Definite assignment.** The compiler analyzes every possible path through your method. If any path reaches a read of the variable without having assigned it first, compilation fails.
- **Compile-time error, not runtime.** The program never starts. The compiler prints: `variable fee might not have been initialized`. No bytecode is produced.
s1_definition.analogy: A bank teller uses a scrap pad to jot down temporary figures while serving a customer. The scrap pad starts blank. The bank's auditor says: you may never read a number off the pad unless you can prove you wrote it there first. If you try to read a blank line, the auditor stops the transaction before it starts. That is the Java compiler refusing to compile code that reads an uninitialized local variable.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Compiler: definite-assignment analysis
  ────────────────────────────────────────

  Case 1: int fee; print(fee);
    Path: [declare] → [read] → NO assignment anywhere → COMPILE ERROR

  Case 2: int fee; if(cond) fee=20; print(fee);
    Path A (true):  [declare] → [assign 20] → [read] → OK
    Path B (false): [declare] → [read] → NOT assigned → COMPILE ERROR

  Case 3: int fee=0; if(cond) fee=20; print(fee);
    Path A (true):  [declare=0] → [assign 20] → [read] → OK
    Path B (false): [declare=0] → [read] → OK (has default 0)
    → COMPILES

  Case 4: int fee; if(cond) fee=20; else fee=0; print(fee);
    Path A (true):  [declare] → [assign 20] → [read] → OK
    Path B (false): [declare] → [assign 0] → [read] → OK
    → COMPILES

  Case 5: int fee; if(bad) throw; fee=20; print(fee);
    Path A (bad):   [declare] → [throw] → path ends, pruned
    Path B (ok):    [declare] → [assign 20] → [read] → OK
    → COMPILES
```

```text
  Comparison: how languages handle uninitialized locals
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  C:      reads garbage from stack       → silent wrong value (dangerous)
  Python: NameError at runtime           → caught late, only on that path
  Java:   compile error, no bytecode     → caught early, all paths checked
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
If you declare a local variable and try to use it without assigning a value, the code does not compile. Java prints the error "variable might not have been initialized" and refuses to produce any bytecode. The program never starts.

The reason is that local variables in Java never receive a default value. This is intentionally different from instance variables, which default to zero, false, or null when the JVM zeroes out the heap memory for a new object. Local variables live on the stack, and instead of zeroing the stack frame at runtime, Java enforces a compile-time rule called definite assignment. The compiler traces every possible execution path through your method, and if any path reaches a read of the variable without having assigned it first, compilation fails.

This is the safest approach among mainstream languages. C lets you read garbage. Python catches it at runtime, but only when that specific line executes. Java catches it at compile time, before the program even starts, and it checks every path, not just the one your test happened to exercise. In banking code this means a transfer method can never silently read an unset fee or amount and move the wrong money.

The fix is straightforward: either initialize the variable at declaration with a sensible default, or make sure every branch of every if, switch, and try-catch assigns the variable before the first read. If a branch throws or returns, the compiler prunes it from the analysis, so only the surviving paths need to assign.

One sentence to remember: local variables get no default, and Java's definite-assignment rule catches the bug at compile time on every path, so the wrong value can never reach runtime.
